The documentation confirms that the namespace `restricted-app` is enforcing a restricted Pod Security Standard (`pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`).

The `restricted` standard requires:
1.  `runAsNonRoot: true` (Pods must run as non-root).
2.  Restricted capabilities (e.g., dropping all unnecessary capabilities).
3.  `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`.

The current workload uses `busybox:1.37.0` and has no `securityContext` defined, which defaults to running as root and having default (broad) capabilities. This is why it is failing admission.

The fix is to patch the Deployment's pod template to meet the `restricted` PSS requirements, which is the smallest change to the workload while respecting the namespace security setting.

I will patch the deployment `app` in namespace `restricted-app` to set the required `securityContext`.

Patch details:
1. Set `securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` on the Pod specification.
2. Set `securityContext.runAsUser` to a non-root user (e.g., 1000).
3. Set `securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`.
4. Drop all capabilities (`securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`).

I will use `kubectl patch` for this.

Pod Security Admission
The Kubernetes [Pod Security Standards](/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/) define
different isolation levels for Pods. These standards let you define how you want to restrict the
behavior of pods in a clear, consistent fashion.

Kubernetes offers a built-in _Pod Security_ admission controller to enforce the Pod Security Standards. Pod security restrictions
are applied at the namespace level when pods are
created.

### Built-in Pod Security admission enforcement

This page is part of the documentation for Kubernetes v.
If you are running a different version of Kubernetes, consult the documentation for that release.

## Pod Security levels

Pod Security admission places requirements on a Pod's [Security
Context](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/security-context/) and other related fields according
to the three levels defined by the [Pod Security
Standards](/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards): `privileged`, `baseline`, and
`restricted`. Refer to the [Pod Security Standards](/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards)
page for an in-depth look at those requirements.

## Pod Security Admission labels for namespaces

control mode you want to use for pod security in each namespace. Kubernetes defines a set of 
labels that you can set to define which of the
